text: Its name was the Trieste.
It didn't look like a submarine.
It looked like a giant metal balloon,
because that's basically what it was.
A huge float filled with petrol,
which is lighter than water,
and hanging underneath it,
a small steel ball for the crew.
Inside that ball were two men,
Swiss engineer Jacques Picard
and U.S. Navy officer Don Walsh.
On the 23rd of January, 1960, they began sinking into the Challenger Deep.
The descent took almost five hours.
It was cold, it was cramped, and at around nine kilometers down, there was a loud bang.
The whole sphere shook.
That's not a good sound.
One of the outer windows had cracked, with a thousand atmospheres waiting outside.
They checked their instruments.
The sphere was holding, so they made a decision that still sounds crazy today.
They kept going.
And they touched the bottom, the first humans ever to reach the deepest place on Earth.
They stayed for about 20 minutes. The landing had stirred up a cloud of fine mud so they
could barely see. Then they started the long ride back up.
Deepest picnic in history.
Then, nobody went back for 52 years. In 2012, film director James Cameron, the man who made
Titanic, dived down alone in a narrow green sub called the Deep Sea Challenger. Since
then, a few more explorers have made it, including Victor Vescovo, the man who found that plastic
bag. Think about that. Twelve people have walked on the moon. Until 2019, only three
had ever been to the Challenger Deep. And when they got there, they found something
nobody expected.
